100% Riesling from the Grand Cru site of Kastelberg, planted over a mix of Schist and sandstone. The grapes are pressed very slowly into wooden barrels to ferment, giving the wine a distinct texture and a full, rounded feel on the palate. The 2022 shows great balance, picked early to retain freshness. Chiseled, mineral and persistently salty with great length and complexity. Of course, this being Durrmann, there is a wire of taught acidity cutting through it all.

The Gran Cerdo natural wines have become ubiquitous staples over the years. Providing such great value and easy drinking it's not hard to see why. We've now added the rosado to the range! It's mainly Tempranillo with a little Garnacha and a splash of some of the grapes that end up in the Blanco. Refreshing red strawberry fruits, with a candied quality, make this one a no-brainer for thirsty party drinkers.

Unrivaled value to be found here in this bottle-fermented fizz out of Catalonia's Cava country. It uses a familiar grape, Xarel-lo, but takes it well away from the style of Spain's most famous sparkling wine by adding plenty of aromatic Muscat and doing it all a la pet-nat. This is an altogether more laid-back style; bubbles that fizz but don't impede your consumption in the slightest, light body, peachy texture and that lovely orange blossom perfume. Hazy, glowing, good-time material.

Simple, straight-up Xarel-lo delivering huge bang-for-buck. Clean, fresh and mineral with little of that peppery aroma and a salty twang in the finish, this is a wine you'll want to stock up on and come back to again and again.

Notte is everything we love about Italian skin-contact wines; the Malvasia & Moscato providing an almost never-ending list of complex aromatics: elderflower, jasmine, lime pith, ginger, tinned peaches, clementine zest and more. The Spergola adding an integrated tannic structure that only improves and becomes further embedded with time. So much going on with this fantastic wine and it really stands up to the heavy Emilia cuisine. Put it on the table with formaggio-laden pasta dishes, salumi and porcetta. Sublime stuff!

Proper Lambrusco-style sparkling red that we describe as being like a summer pudding in liquid form. Lots of little inky black berries, a tart lick of acid and something a bit creamy and lactic, with a nicely upfront, grippy tannic structure and frothy bubble. There’s a real savoury, slightly vegetal character here that makes it a must with salumi and the rich, meat-heavy cuisine of Emilia-Romagna. It's in this context that sparkling red wine truly makes sense! For us, this is one of the best out there.

An entry-level selection that immediately claims the plaudit of best-priced orange wine in the house. This is Falanghina with a mixture of the grapes direct-pressed (like a regular white) and some left to macerate on the skins (a la orange) leaving a golden glow and just a modest mouthful of grippy tannins. Ripe, quince-y stone fruits and smoky/nutty flavours jostle together in loose harmony. Very tasty stuff and such bang for buck.

This is his direct-press Aligoté, given a slow 24-48 hour press in his antique basket press, which gives texture and body to the wine. It has electric acidity and incredibly pure fruit. Drinking well already but this one will only benefit from some cellar time if you have the patience to lay it down.

The Crème de Tête 2012 was made from grapes harvested the third week of December "when the moon was in the constellation of Leo, a fire constellation that brings power and plenitude". Alain sprays some mineral (silica based) biodynamic preparations to help the shrivelled grapes hold onto the vines so late into the season – reaching extreme concentration (the unicorn Crème de Tête 2005 was harvested during the last days of December!). Aged for eight years in both oak and acacia barrels, this is fuller and richer than the 2011 and 2013, viscous on the palate and slightly hidden at opening, it de

A fantastic new Cabernet Franc cuvée made using grapes from Mikael Bouges and his more limestone-heavy terroir in Faverolles. The fruit is destemmed and sees a long, three-month maceration before being aged in barrel for 18 months. Aromatically this is a textbook example of the grape; plush, brightly-toned notes of red berries, charred capsicum and ground coffee are vibrant and upfront. On the palate the wine is glossy, with deep, sumptuous fruit and gentle bitters leading into detailed granular tannins and a stony, mineral backbone. A superb new addition to Noëlla's repertoire that stands apa

Peppercorn spice and deep fruits leap from the glass, the texture of the wine is beautifully soft and silky, with integrated, lightly gripping tannic structure. There is a rusty, iron-like mineral quality beneath it all, that really shows itself in the long, stony finish. A truly elegant wine that demonstrates the complexity of its old-vine origin. Reflecting the heat of a scorching vintage, with little rain, the structure is bolder and more concentrated than previous vintages. 100% Gamay from the Guerin’s prized plot of 50 year-old, massal selection vines, planted over sandy, decomposed grani

Another négociant wine, this time using Bergeron, a highly obscure strain of Roussanne that is found in the alpine region of Savoie. Macerated on the skins and aged in barrel, it is is ripe and exotic on the nose, with dry tea-like tannins. Incredibly delicate, alluring and one of Bouju's harder to track down cuvées. Plus a little bit of trivia: the label was designed by non other than elusive winemaker Aurélien Lefort.

Chinato is perhaps Piemonte’s most famous digestif. Traditionally made with aged Barolo, it takes its name from the bark of quinine (or “China”) tree, which is the chief botanical here. Vergano prefers to use a younger wine from Barbaresco, the tannins not as firm, the perfume a little more lifted. The china bark lends the wine tea-like tannins, while herbs and spices like cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, coriander, bay, ginseng and rhubarb provide warmth and real interest. There is no better way to end a meal.

notes: THREE is an amer, a bittersweet digestif in the French tradition, it is the third in our single batch line of botanical spirits. The Single Batch line allows us to discover and experiment with new recipes and production methods. It provides us the freedom to discover new flavors and aromas, play with different types of macerations, distillations, aging, and more. Forthave Spirits started as two friends making small batches of spirits and tracing them back to their herbal, medicinal roots. If you’re unfamiliar with Château Magdelaine, it’s likely because this Saint-Émilion estate no longer exists, with 2011 being their final vintage. It was owned by the Moueix family, who also own Pétrus and Trotanoy in Pomerol. The Magdelaine vineyards sit next to Ausone, one of the most revered names in all of Bordeaux. Like at Ausone, the area’s limestone soils give Magdelaine a fresh, defined style. A key difference, along with more merlot and less oak at Magdelaine, is the fact that 1981 Ausone costs 4x as much.

Bryan Deleu is an up-and-coming name to know in the Northern Rhône. After studying architecture, working as a hotel maître d', and training at a series of renowned wineries, Bryan purchased a small plot of neglected vineyard land in Saint-Joseph in 2018. After clearing and terracing the land himself, Bryan planted syrah on the region’s granite slopes. Exorde is his flagship. It’s textbook Northern Rhône syrah, meaning savory, smoky, and powerfully aromatic. Tastes like: Blackberry, violets, smoke, cracked pepper. How to drink: Alongside lamb chops, steak, or a winter stew.

wine: Scar of the Sea, SLO Coast Chardonnay 2024
notes: On California’s central coast, fog and cool breezes from the Pacific help produce chardonnay that’s fresh, citrusy, and a bit salty. That’s certainly the case at Scar of the Sea, whose home vineyard - a key source of this wine - is just one mile from the ocean. Mikey and Gina Giugni farm it biodynamically, and age their chardonnay for nearly two years in barrel before bottling. The result is a white wine that’s richly textured without being oaky. Tastes like: Green apple, lemon curd, biscuits, sea spray. How to drink: Chilled with shellfish, roast chicken, or linguine with clams.

The husband-and-wife team of Matt Naumann and Audra Chapman launched Newfound in the Sierra Foothills in 2016. They wanted to explore the potential of making fresh, easy-drinking red wines from Mediterranean grapes in this part of northern California. Gravels is their flagship. An equal blend of grenache and carignan, it showcases the juicy fruit and lifted aromatics of the former, as well as the firm structure and savory notes of carignan. Tastes like: Raspberry, lavender, sage, black pepper. How to drink: Lightly chilled with burgers, grilled sausages, or margherita pizza.

wine: Domaine de la Giraudière, Saumur-Champigny Rouge 'Les Meuniers' 2024
notes: In the Loire Valley, third-generation winemaker Fabrice Esnault crafts pure, unoaked wines from chenin blanc and cabernet franc. This example of the latter comes from the limestone slopes of Saumur-Champigny. It’s a juicy, medium-bodied red with cab franc’s hallmark earthy, spice-laden aromatics on full display. Tastes like: Blackberry, violets, tobacco leaf, black pepper. How to drink: Lightly chilled with barbecue ribs, pepperoni pizza, or vegetarian lasagna.

wine: Terralibera, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore 2025
notes: Gian Mario Bongini left a career in corporate finance to pursue one in winemaking, leaving Milan for the rural region of Le Marche. There, Gian Mario organically farms one grape, verdicchio, on two hillside vineyards a half-hour inland from the Adriatic. This white grape makes forgettable wines in many parts of Italy, but in the small area of Castelli di Jesi, it yields one of Italy’s great light, crisp, coastal whites. Tastes like: Pear, lemon zest, salted almond, jasmine. How to drink: Chilled with grilled shrimp or fried calamari.

wine: Domaine Julien Cruchandeau, Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits Rouge 'Les Valancons' 2024
notes: For the last 20 years, Julien Cruchandeau has been at the forefront of bringing high-quality winemaking to less heralded parts of Burgundy. That started in Bouzeron, where he focused on aligoté, with some initial assistance from the legendary Aubert de Villaine of DRC. Julien then moved on to the hills above Nuits-Saint-Georges, which is where he organically farms this pinot noir. It’s robust and earthy, while still showing Julien’s bright, elegant touch in the cellar. Tastes like: Blackberry, baking spices, grilled mushrooms. How to drink: Alongside roast chicken or mushroom risotto.

At Tregole, Sophie Conte crafts wines from the highest-altitude vineyards in all of Chianti Classico. The first-generation winemaker takes advantage of the area’s cool nights and limestone soils to produce a fresh, floral, lithe style of sangiovese. That’s on display in this particularly food-friendly Tuscan red. Tastes like: Red cherry, tomato leaf, violets. How to drink: Lightly chilled with spaghetti pomodoro, pizza, or anything with red sauce.

Pedro Rodriguez farms old vines of local grape varieties, which grow on dramatically steep vineyards in Ribeira Sacra, an area of Galicia in northwestern Spain. While Ribeira Sacra is nearly synonymous with reds made from mencia, Pedro makes this richly textured white wine primarily from the godello grape. High altitude, cool nights, and stainless steel-aging keep the medium-bodied white fresh and smoky. Tastes like: Pear, lemon zest, chamomile, fennel. How to drink: Chilled with scallops, fish tacos, or roast chicken.

Since launching his own label 15 years ago in a cellar in downtown Cape Town, Duncan Savage has established himself as one of the most exciting winemakers in South Africa. His white wine style is all about freshness and bright acidity. For this 100% sauvignon blanc bottling, those traits are amplified even more by windy, high-elevation vineyard sites around the Stellenbosch region outside of Cape Town. Tastes like: Grapefruit, lemon zest, white flowers, sea salt. How to drink: Chilled with oysters, fried seafood, or citrusy salads.

wine: Chateau de L’Étoile, Côtes du Jura Rouge 2024
notes: Chateau de L’Étoile dates back centuries, but its current chapter begins in 2024. That’s when Louis Fourrier, the son of Burgundy legend Jean-Marie Fourrier, took over the estate. In the future, Louis plans to split his time between the Jura and his family’s iconic domaine in Gevrey-Chambertin, but for now, his focus is squarely on L’Étoile. 2024 was a remarkably low-yielding vintage, and Louis only produced about one-quarter of what he intends to when conditions are ideal. wine: Hope Well, Eola-Amity Hills Chenin Blanc 2025
notes: Mimi Casteel grew up in the vines of the Willamette Valley, as her father Ted Casteel is the founder of famed Oregon winery Bethel Heights. Now, Mimi runs her own project in the Willamette, making natural wines at Hope Well. Mimi is extremely passionate about her land, with organic and biodynamic farming only telling a small part of the story. The result is a range of expressive, site-specific pinot noir and chenin blanc. This example of the latter is a vibrant, salty, super fresh white wine. Only a little more than 1000 bottles were produced in total. Tastes like: Peach, lemon zest, honeysuck

Beaujolais gets no better than Lapierre. Largely responsible for both Beaujolais and natural wine breaking into the mainstream, Lapierre has long been the benchmark for the serious side of gamay. This new release of their flagship red is earthy, peppery, and nuanced, without sacrificing anything in the way of freshness or ‘chillability’.

wine: Forteresse de Berrye, Saumur Blanc 'Les Bourgères' 2023
notes: Forteresse de Berrye is an ancient military fort, which happens to sit on some of the best land for chenin blanc in the Loire Valley. Gilles Colinet saw its potential, and has been reviving both the land and castle since 2019. Bourgères comes from a plot of organic chenin grown in chalky limestone soils, which contribute a crisp, minerally character and notable freshness. Tastes like: Pear, lemon zest, sea salt, jasmine. How to drink: Chilled with soft cheeses or rich seafood dishes like pan-seared scallops.

Jean-Claude Lapalu is one of the great natural winemakers in Beaujolais. Following in the footsteps of Lapierre, Foillard, and Métras, he helped show the wine scene in Paris (and then the world) what Beaujolais was capable of. Based in the area of Brouilly, Jean-Claude has an abundance of old vines, which give his Beaujolais structure and complexity to go along with gamay’s classic bright fruit and floral aromatics. Tastes like: Black cherry, violets, white pepper. How to drink: A versatile chilled red that works with cheese and charcuterie or even grilled fish.

wine: Guiberteau, Saumur Blanc 'Les Moulins - Chai de la Dive' 2024
notes: The rolling hills of Saumur produce many of the greatest chenin blanc wines in the Loire Valley. Nobody masters the area’s limestone soils like Romain Guiberteau. A protege of Nady Foucault at the legendary Clos Rougeard, Romain ages this organic chenin in stainless steel, which yields a particularly fresh, mineral, vivid white wine. Tastes like: Pear, honeycomb, smoke. How to drink: Chilled with a goat cheese salad or lemony seafood dishes.

It’s fresh, citrusy, and salty today, but also complex and capable of aging.

notes: Anna Espelt runs her family’s winery in Empordà, north of Barcelona on the Catalan side of the Pyrenees. While the area is better known for its reds, Anna believes it's equally capable of producing high-quality whites. She crafts this fresh, notably herbaceous white primarily from garnacha blanc, which she farms organically in this beautiful part of northeastern Spain. From the Basque Country on the northern coast of Spain, txakolina is an absolutely ideal warm weather white wine. It’s light, tart, and salty, with the kind of brisk acidity that makes it perfect with fresh seafood or refreshing on its own. Tastes like: Green apple, salty limes, cut grass. How to drink: A perfect brunch wine, or any other time of day with spicy seafood soup.

This sparkling wine is made from a grape called glera, which Bisol sources from lush, green hillsides between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy. Dry and refreshing, it’s a crisp, floral, easy-drinking alternative to Cava. Tastes like: Pear, salty lemons, and white flowers. How to drink: Cold on its own, or with anything salty and fried.

Agustí Torello Roca makes our favorite sparkling wines in Spain. He produces this bottling with macabeu and xarel-lo in Penedès. While those are the most common grapes and location for Cava production, Roca crafts this natural sparkler in the ancestral method, resulting in an effervescent pét-nat rosé that’s light and highly refreshing. Tastes like: Wild strawberry, citrus peel, and salt. How to drink: Cold, on its own, or with charcuterie and fried snacks.

wine: Château Peyrassol, Côtes de Provence Rosé 'Cuvée des Commanderie' 2023
notes: Peyrassol has been around for 800 years, so as you might imagine, its wines very much reflect those of the region as a whole. For Provencal rosé, that means light, pale pink, easy-drinking wines made from a blend of cinsault and grenache. Peyrassol’s organic vineyards are a stone’s throw from the Mediterranean coast, giving their rosé notable saltiness and freshness.

Les Baux-de-Provence is a tiny French wine region with just 12 producers. Those domaines, however, carry serious weight in the world of fine wine. Domaine de Trévallon, Domaine Hauvette, and Henri Milan all call Les Baux home. A more recent entrant making waves is Domaine Fontchêne, which is meticulously overseen by Henri Milan’s nephew, René Milan. René makes this juicy, lean, salty rosé from grenache, along with a small portion of cinsault and mourvedre. Tastes like: Strawberry, peach, herbs, and salt. How to drink: Chilled, with grilled fish, salad, or on its own.

wine: Maison A&S, Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Beaune Rouge 2023
notes: Longtime friends Alexandre Aires and Pierre-Alexandre Soltana launched Maison A&S (Aires & Soltana) in 2018. However, the duo are certainly not new to the Burgundy wine scene. Pierre-Alexandre is the head of viticulture at Comtes Lafon and Alexandre is the cellar master at Thibault Liger-Belair. In 2021, they acquired a winemaking facility in the Hautes-Côtes de Beaune. This tart, earthy, ultra-fresh Red Burgundy comes from old vines surrounding their winery. Tastes like: Raspberry, black pepper, dried leaves. How to drink: A versatile, chillable red that works with burgers and sausages, pizza

Jakob Moise, who previously worked under the iconic Frank Cornelissen in Sicily, is part of a new generation of German winemakers showing how elegant spätburgunder (German for pinot noir) can be. In the southern region of Baden - the same area where Wasenhaus makes some of Germany’s most sought-after wines - Jakob makes this bright, perfumed, exceptionally easy-drinking expression of pinot noir. Tastes like: Red cherry, rose petals, white pepper. How to drink: Chilled with cheese and charcuterie, roast chicken, or even grilled salmon.

This light red wine from the German region of Württemberg is crafted in the same fresh, energetic style that’s made Roterfaden a darling of the natural wine world. Olympia Samara and Hannes Hoffmann blend pinot noir with blaufränkisch (known in Germany as lemberger) to craft a wine that’s tart, smoky, and an absolutely ideal chilled summer red. Tastes like: Cherry Jolly Rancher, smoke, dried herbs. How to drink: Chilled this summer, in the same rotation as Beaujolais and light Jura reds.

wine: Domaine du Chancelier, Bourgogne Côte d'Or Rouge 'En Coulezain' Vieilles Vignes 2022

The Colle Gaio of Antonio Pulcini has cult-status among Italian wine insiders. The reasons are many: unique farming and production methods, tiny volumes, releases debuting with decades of age, a reclusive winemaker who sells allocations primarily from the cellar’s front door, and the list goes on. But the takeaway is this: if you enjoy the iconic whites of Miani, Valentini, or Gravner, then this is a rare opportunity to try another singular Italian white wine.

That vineyard, however, happens to be Montestefano, home to some of the greatest dirt in all of Piedmont, and their red wines are as compelling as they are scarce. Rivella is an old-school producer, but while their nebbiolo has density and a deeply savory quality, it’s also fresh, silky, and refined. In other words, it’s absolutely delicious.

Jérome Fornerot’s family has roots in Burgundy dating back a half-millenium, but he only launched his own domaine in the early ‘00s. Since then, his whites have become some of the best sources of value in Burgundy. This fresh, smoky white comes from a single plot in Santenay, a village that borders Chassagne-Montrachet and Fornerot’s hometown of Saint-Aubin. Tastes like: White peach, smoke, salted almond. How to drink: Chilled with fresh seafood or linguine in clam sauce.

When it comes to wine regions poised to explode in popularity over the next few years, the Dão in Portugal is near the top of the list. One of the winemakers leading the charge is Parisian-born Antonio Madeira. Madeira makes this juicy, earthy, medium-bodied red from a field blend of local grape varieties, including alfrocheiro, baga, jaen, and many more. Less than 1000 cases are produced annually. Tastes like: Blackberry, violets, leather, cinnamon. How to drink: With lamb chops, sauteed mushrooms, or a winter stew.

Françoise and Stéphane Dief launched Clos Manou in their garage in the ‘90s. So compared to most of their neighbors on the Left Bank of Bordeaux, they’re new to the scene. They make just two wines, both from their organic plots of cabernet sauvignon and merlot. Compared to their ‘Grand Vin’, this features more merlot in the blend, yielding rich, round red wine that’s delicious right away. Tastes like: Plum, licorice, vanilla, cigar box. How to drink: Perfect with red meat or a rich, savory risotto.

Julien Courtois handcrafts small quantities of natural wine in a remote part of the Loire Valley between Vouvray and Sancerre. Instead of chenin or sauvignon blanc, as you’d find in those two areas, Julien instead focuses on local grapes like menu pineau and genouillet. Despite the esoteric grape varieties and super-limited production, Courtois has gained a following in natural wine circles around the world. The Autochtone is a white wine that showcases Julien’s vibrant, head-turning style. Made entirely from romorantin, it’s ripe and nutty, reminiscent of savory, textured whites from the Jura

In the Mosel region of Germany, the young and exceptionally talented Moritz Hoffman took over for the late Daniel Vollenweider in 2022. While Daniel was best known for his otherworldly off-dry wines, Moritz has a particular knack for dry riesling. Elegant, herbal, and high acid, this dry white puts that on display.

Fresh. Biodynamic. Immediately enjoyable. These aren’t the first words we typically associate with Bordeaux. And yet that’s exactly how we’d describe the red wines from Michel Théron at Clos du Jaugueyron. His small-production wines are bright and herbaceous, while still showcasing the Left Bank’s calling card notes of dark fruits and savory spices.

Not far from the borders of both Slovenia and Hungary, Christoph Neumeister makes some of Austria’s most singular white wines. Along with pinot gris and sauvignon blanc, he organically farms weissburgunder (pinot blanc) on the region’s remarkably steep slopes. The result is a medium-bodied white wine that would be fun to put in a lineup with unoaked chardonnay.

David Trousselle is located in the generally unknown village of Orches in Burgundy. But when you consider that Orches is located directly between Saint-Aubin and Saint-Romain, and is walking distance from both, it’s less surprising that Trousselle makes excellent wines from the area’s limestone soils. He crafts this bright, earthy red entirely from gamay, resulting in a style that brings to mind serious Beaujolais. Only about 150 cases are produced annually.

Envínate is arguably the most exciting producer in Spain today. While most of their wines come from the Canary Islands and Galicia, ‘Albahra’ is made in the southerly region of Almansa. Its location and grapes - garnacha tintorera and the nearly extinct, moravia agria - are obscure, but the fresh, earthy red will be in the wheelhouse of anyone who enjoys chilled reds.

notes: The young José Joaquín Ballesteros makes wines in a southern Spanish village best known for its clay amphora tanks. At Llámalo (pronounced "yah-mah-low"), he organically farms local grape varieties like cencibel, moravia, and bobal to make this smooth, aromatic red wine. The ‘GR-10’ is floral, peppery, and juicy. A versatile, medium-bodied red wine. Tastes like: Plum, roses, thyme, black pepper. The cool, high-altitude vineyards here yield fresher, lighter, easier-drinking expressions of nebbiolo than you’d find a couple hours south in Barolo and Barbaresco. Fast forward to present, and he’s producing nearly a dozen different wines from organic vineyards in and around Chablis. This white wine is the flagship. In southern Spain, the Cerdán family makes natural wines that are antithesis to the nondescript, mass-produced juice that the Jumilla region was long known for. They farm monastrell (Spanish for mourvèdre) organically and biodynamically, utilizing the area’s high-elevation vineyard sites to produce a juicy, rich red wine with a remarkable level of freshness and balance considering the near desert-like conditions. Tastes like: Blackberry, violets, thyme, dark chocolate. How to drink: Ideal with paella, lamb chops, or all kinds of BBQ.

wine: Pain-Perdu, Chardonnay Santa Barbara County 'Rancho San Julian Vineyard' 2023
notes: This is the inaugural release from Pain-Perdu in Santa Barbara. Winemaker Fabien Castel is using the cool, coastal climate along the Pacific to produce elegant, earthy pinot noir and chardonnay. This is his only white wine thus far. Textured, nuanced, and notably salty, it would be a fun bottle to put in a blind tasting alongside unoaked White Burgundy. Tastes like: Green apple, smoke, salted hazelnuts. How to drink: Not too cold with roast chicken, sushi, or mushroom risotto.

notes: We’ve long been big fans of all Champagne from the Bérêche brothers, but even for them, this wine stands out. Immaculate farming, barrel aging, nearly 7 years on the lees, and one of the great Champagne vintages of the past quarter-century - it all combines to create a rich, layered wine that’s one of the very best we’ve ever had from Bérêche.

Dominique Roger is one of the greatest winemakers in Sancerre. Dominique’s family has been making wine in the village of Bué for centuries, and his high-elevation vineyards are some of the best in the region. At Domaine du Carrou, he hard-harvests those organic plots to make precise, deeply textured wines that remind us of top-class Chablis. A lot of Sancerre is pretty straightforward, and to be honest, it can get boring after a while. Dominique’s ‘La Jouline’ is a changeup. Its old vines and touch of oak give it more weight and richness than the other wines in this lineup.

wine: Domaine Denis Mortet, Gevrey-Chambertin 'Mes Cinq Terroirs' 2018
notes: Denis Mortet achieved star status in Burgundy in the ‘90s. With the legendary Henri Jayer as his longtime mentor, Denis made Red Burgundy that was lush and powerful. Since taking over, Denis’ son, Arnaud, has evolved the winemaking towards more elegance and detail. The wines, which never lost the Mortet intensity and ultra-expressive fruit, have never been better. ‘Mes Cinq Terroirs’ is the Mortet flagship. It’s a classic picture of the deep, earthy character of Gevrey-Chambertin, as well as an illustration of Arnaud’s silky, refined style. This is collectible Red Burgundy through and through.

notes: On his family’s historic estate outside Corsica's capital city of Ajaccio, Jean-Charles Abbatucci biodynamically farms indigenous varieties, some of which he helped bring back from the edge of extinction. Tastes like: Raspberry, chamomile, tarragon, sea salt. How to drink: Cold with sushi, cheese and charcuterie, or grilled chicken.

As a former management consultant, Anatole de la Brosse did what you might expect when he launched his own winery in 2018. He sought guidance from the Loire’s ultimate ‘consultant’, Nady Foucault of Clos Rougeard. Organic and biodynamic from the outset, his cabernet franc is deeper and more complex than most red wines from Saumur-Champigny. It’s also rarer, as only about 1000 cases are made annually. Tastes like: Blackberry, grilled bell peppers, cigar box. How to drink: Pair with charcuterie, hearty red sauce dishes, or lean cuts of steak.

wine: Mas des Capitelles, Faugeres Vieilles Vignes 2021
notes: The Languedoc produces a ton of wine. More, in fact, than any other region in France. But frankly, most of it isn’t worth your time. The wines of Jean Laugé are notable exceptions. In the dry, rugged hills of Faugères, Jean organically farms old vines of grape varieties like mourvèdre, grenache, and syrah, which form the blend in this vibrant, full-bodied, savory red wine. Tastes like: Blueberry, violet, leather, black pepper. How to drink: Ideal with chicken and chorizo paella, or all things BBQ.

Las Pedreras is a new project from the mountains outside Madrid, the same area you’ll find Comando G and Raúl Pérez. It’s run by Bárbara Requejo Frutos, who previously worked at Château Haut-Brion in Bordeaux and Pierre Peters in Champagne. Back in Spain, she organically farms just one grape variety: garnacha (grenache). Bright, herbal, and floral, ‘Los Arroyuelos’ is a perfect window into Bárbara’s elegant style. Tastes like: Raspberry, lavender, thyme, black pepper. How to drink: Lightly chilled with just about anything on the grill.

At Guímaro, Pedro Rodriguez is making some of the most exciting wines in Spain today. The family producer farms old vines of local grape varieties, which grow on dramatically steep vineyards in Ribeira Sacra, an area of Galicia in northwestern Spain. Pedro makes this richly textured white wine from godello. High altitude, cool nights, and stainless steel-aging keep it the midweight white tasting fresh and mineral Tastes like: Pear, lemon zest, chamomile, fennel. How to drink: Chilled with scallops, fish tacos, or roast chicken.

wine: Terralibera, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi 'Insieme' 2023
notes: Gian Mario Bongini left a career in finance to pursue one in winemaking, leaving Milan for the rural region of Le Marche. There, Gian Mario organically farms one grape, verdicchio, on two hillside vineyards a half-hour inland from the Adriatic. This white grape makes forgettable wines in many parts of Italy, but in the small area of Castelli di Jesi, it yields one of Italy’s great, crisp coastal whites. Tastes like: Ripe peach, salted almond, jasmine. How to drink: As a unique alternative to Chablis, or anytime there are oysters on the table.

Gruner veltliner is Austria’s most common grape, and it runs the stylistic gamut from light and easy to dense and opulent. Our favorite versions, however, are somewhere in between. Lithe and pure yet intensely mineral and full of energy. Barbara Öhlzelt epitomizes this take on the grape. Old vines and barrel aging yield a gruner with texture and depth over a lightweight frame. Tastes like: Ripe pear, white pepper, chives, salt. How to drink: Cold with sushi, grilled fish, or roasted veggies.

Liguria doesn’t have the reputation of coastal Italian wine regions like Campania, Sicily, Tuscany, Sardinia, and so on. The small area south of Piedmont is better known for plenty of other things - the beaches of the Riviera, Monet paintings, Cinque Terre, and pesto. With all that said, we tried this Ligurian vermentino recently, and it’s absolutely worth a shot. It’s made by Fabio Lambruschi, who is still helped in the vineyard by his 93 year-old father Ottaviano, on a dramatic hillside overlooking the Mediterranean Sea. While some vermentino can be waxy, oaky, or bitter, this is different.

wine: Pierre Girardin, Bourgogne Blanc 'Eclat de Calcaire' 2022
notes: Pierre-Vincent Girardin is still in his 20’s. On the flip side of that coin: he’s the 13th generation of his family to make wine, he’s been roaming cellars in Burgundy since the age of five, and he took over only the best vineyard plots from his highly respected father. So, his rapid rise to stardom didn’t come out of left field. This new release - made primarily with grapes from Pierre’s hometown of Meursault - showcases his crisp, elegant, salty style of White Burgundy. Today, it’s available for about 1/10th the price of some of Pierre’s other white wines.

In the Mosel, Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler organically farm tiny, terraced plots of old vines to make this dry riesling . It's light and pure, with tart salty notes that make it particularly refreshing.

Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler make this bone-dry sparkling wine with old-vine riesling using the same method as Champagne. It's a lithe, refreshing, limited-release bubbly from one of the most exciting producers in the Mosel today.

Weiser-Künstler is currently making some of the most exciting riesling in all of Germany. The husband-and-wife duo of Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler farm ancient vines - doing everything by hand - to produce small quantities of old-school rieslings in the Mosel. While each vineyard has its own distinctive identity, the wines all share a throughline of delicacy and high-acid energy. Another attribute they share in spades is value (for now). The husband-and-wife duo of Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler run one of the most intentional, exciting wineries in the Mosel today. They craft this Kabinett riesling from ungrafted, 100 year-old vines that are the heart and soul of the estate. Minty, smoky, intensely mineral notes meet plenty of ripe fruit, all in a wine that clocks in at 8% alcohol. Special stuff.

Stefan Vetter is one of the most exciting producers in Germany today. In the cool, hilly region of Franken, he makes high-acid, salty, ultra-drinkable white wines from the local sylvaner grape. Elegant and lithe, this Grand Cru bottling encompasses his style perfectly.

Stefan Vetter is arguably the most exciting white wine producer in Germany today. His sylvaners are simultaneously elegant and bracingly tart. They pack a mind-bending level of texture and nuance into a lithe, airy frame. The 'Himmelslücke' has subtle floral notes and less subtle citrus ones, all layered over deep, salty minerality. An absolutely delicious white wine.

This sharp, salty white comes from the German region of Franken, where Stefan Vetter is making truly electric wines. This 'Premier Cru' bottling is low enough alcohol enough to be exceptionally easy-drinking, yet concentrated and textured enough to serve as an alternative to top-level Chablis.
Rotling is the German word for a rosé made from a blend of red and white grapes. In this case, that means pinot noir and müller-thurgau. The resulting rosé is pale-colored, salty, and easy-drinking.

Jean-Louis Grippat is one of the great producers in the history of the Northern Rhone. While he retired a quarter-century ago - ‘98 is the last vintage he ever bottled - his wines remain the high-water mark for traditional Saint-Joseph. Like Gentaz in Cote-Rotie and Verset in Cornas, bottles from Grippat are an increasingly rare look at a past era. Meaty, savory, and intensely aromatic, with Burgundy-like finesse. These are true reference-point wines for any fan of old-school syrah.

wine: Sofia, Etna Bianco 'La Vigna di Gioacchino' 2022
notes: Carricante, a grape variety almost exclusively grown in the volcanic soils of Mount Etna in Sicily, yields salty, crisp white wines that can be reminiscent of textured Chablis. Carmelo Sofia and his sister, Valentina, make this carricante from organic, old vines on the volcano’s northern slope. Two days of skin contact yields a rich, ripe-fruited expression of Etna Bianco. Tastes like: Apricot, lemon meringue, smoke. How to drink: Cold alongside hard cheeses, anchovy toast, or linguine with clams.

wine: Cati Ribot, Ve d'Avior Blanc 'Son Llebre' 2022
notes: Mallorca doesn’t have the winemaking pedigree of some other Mediterranean islands, but that’s beginning to change. The reason? Cati Ribot. After training as a sommelier in Barcelona, Cati returned to her native Mallorca, and began experimenting with the Spanish island’s extremely esoteric, native grape varieties. A decade or so later, her textured, aromatic whites are gaining a following in natural wine circles around the world. Cati makes this skin-contact white with grapes like giró ros and malvasía de banyalbufar planted in the winery’s backyard. Tastes like: Apricot, orange zest, sea salt.

wine: Azienda Agricola Sofia, Etna Rosso 'La Vigna di Gioacchino' 2021
notes: Mount Etna is a unique place to produce wine. High altitudes, constant Mediterranean winds, a giant (highly active) volcano. Making wine here takes passion, which Carmelo and Valentina Sofia most certainly possess. So much so that - until 2017 - their wines were just for personal consumption. Fortunately, the brother-and-sister duo began offering their organic nerello mascalese more broadly, which brings this fresh, earthy red wine to us now. Tastes like: Cherry, roses, sea salt, leather. How to drink: Alongside eggplant parm, smoked meats, or rich red sauce pastas.

While Las Jaras has a celebrity co-founder in Eric Wareheim, this California-based natural producer is truly passionate about quality winemaking. Eric and winemaker Joel Burt craft this tart, energetic rosé from organic, hand-harvested grape varieties native to Italy, like sangiovese, dolcetto, and barbera. Tastes like: Wild raspberry, violets, lemon zest, fennel. How to drink: Cold while lounging by the pool, or alongside snacks at a picnic or BBQ.

Aligoté is very much having a moment. Long thought of as chardonnay’s simpler counterpart in Burgundy, it’s now yielding exceptional whites all over the region. David Trousselle’s organic bottling is a prime example. He makes this toasty, salty wine from hand-harvested aligoté just outside Saint-Aubin in the Cote de Beaune. Tastes like: Pear, honeysuckle, smoked almonds. How to drink: Chilled on its own, or alongside simply prepared seafood.

In the Loire Valley, between Vouvray and Sancerre, Pascal Potaire and Moses Gadouche specialize in natural sparkling wines. While their range of pét-nats run the gamut stylistically, ‘Pynoz’ is as tangy and easy-drinking as they come. The lightly sparkling rosé is made from an equal blend of old-vine pinot noir and the local pineau d’aunis. Tastes like: Raspberry, wildflowers, tamarind. How to drink: Cold with grilled veggies, cheese and charcuterie, or salty snacks.

The Cornu family has lived in the Burgundian town of Echevronne since the thirteenth century, and you’ll find their winery there today. So, it’s safe to say that they understand the area pretty darn well. They make this round, subtly toasty White Burgundy from a single vineyard in Savigny-les-Beaune. wine: Wenzlau Vineyard, Santa Rita Hills Chardonnay 'The Drawing Board' 2016
notes: In 2011, Cindy and Bill Wenzlau acquired a rugged, foggy plot of land in Santa Barbara on the banks of the Santa Ynez River. Working with Justin Willett (Tyler Wines), they utilized the area’s cool, marine-accented climate to produce earthy, restrained examples of pinot noir and chardonnay. This white - originally crisp and mineral-driven - has taken on more savory, nutty flavors with age. Tastes like: Pear, roasted hazelnuts, honeysuckle, ocean breeze. How to drink: Not too cold alongside rich seafood dishes or salty cheeses.

wine: Mira do Ó, Dão Vidente Tinto 2019
notes: Few people illustrate the current renaissance in Portuguese wine better than Nuno Mira do Ó. Nuno scours the length of the country in search of old, forgotten parcels of local grape varieties. He then pursues a light-touch approach in order to let those grapes express themselves in the bottle. This spicy, silky red wine is a blend of hand-picked grapes - jaen, alfrocheiro, touriga nacional, to name a few - from the granite soils of the Dão. Tastes like: Wild cherry, violet, leather, cinnamon. How to drink: With BBQ, mushroom katsu, or a hearty stew.

Jacquère is the most planted grape in the Savoie, a region better known for skiing and fondue than high-quality wine. But in the hands of David Dupasquier, the fifth-generation to run his family winery, you’ll see exactly what this alpine grape is capable of. It’s crisp, minerally, and highly refreshing, an ideal alternative to Muscadet or Chablis. Tastes like: Lemon zest, toast, sea salt, smoke. How to drink: Cold with crudo, oysters, or soft cheeses.

If you’re not familiar, Envínate is arguably the most exciting producer in Spain. And if you are, then know that these wines are as good as any reds they’ve ever released. They’re all made naturally in the remote (absolutely gorgeous) region of Ribeira Sacra in Galicia. These are savory, spicy red wines that are wildly undervalued considering the quality. More savory than the 'Viñas de Aldea' and less weighty than their single-parcel wines, this small-production bottling is fresh, earthy, and highly versatile with food.

Morgon produces some of the most savory, deep, full-bodied wines in Beaujolais. The area’s granite-rich soils, which the young Quentin Harel farms organically, yields a particularly grippy, concentrated expression of gamay. Tastes like: Ripe plum, violet, fresh-tilled soil. How to drink: Slightly chilled with burgers, pizza, or BBQ chicken.

'Les Petites Fleurs' is made entirely from gamay, and tastes like a particularly deep and peppery version of Beaujolais.

Tissot is a benchmark in the Jura for a wide range of wines. This is perhaps the most unusual. Chardonnay Rose is a very rare, pink grape variety that Tissot makes in miniscule quantities. It yields a white wine that’s floral, toasty, and herbal - it’s unlike any other wine out there, from the Jura or otherwise. Tastes like: Citrus zest, fennel, acacia, brioche. How to drink: Chilled with herb and spice-heavy dishes like falafel.

This is the flagship white wine from arguably the most important producer in the Jura: Stéphane Tissot. Salty and toasty yet crisp and detailed, ‘Patchwork’ always serves as a clear reminder that the Jura is just an hour’s drive east from the heart of the Cote de Beaune. Tastes like: Ripe pear, sea salt, roasted hazelnuts. How to drink: Not too cold anytime you want an alternative to salty, textured White Burgundy.

notes: 700 miles from the Spanish mainland off the coast of Morocco, the Canary Islands are home to some of the most distinctive, just plain delicious white wines in all of Spain. While the volcanic island of Tenerife has become a natural wine hotspot in recent years, Borja Pérez Gonzalez’s family has been making wine here for the last century. Borja makes this salty, savory white from old vines of the local grape, listan blanco. Tastes like: Peach, smoke, sea salt, lemon curd. How to drink: Chilled with all types of seafood.

wine: Rubén Díaz Viticultor, Cebreros Doré Chasselas 2022
notes: Skin-contact chasselas from the mountains of central Spain. It sounds… strange. But in the hands of Rubén Díaz, the result is a delicate orange wine that’s more mineral-driven and refreshing than funky. Díaz has been a quality pioneer of Gredos, the rugged area west of Madrid, for the last 20 years. He only makes 200 cases of this chasselas, a high-acid grape variety typically reserved for the alpine slopes of Switzerland. Tastes like: Apricot, orange zest, sea salt. How to drink: Cold with curry, falafel, or a big cheese board.

On dramatically steep vineyards in Ribeira Sacra in northwestern Spain, Pedro Rodriguez hand-crafts bright red wines from the local grape, mencía. The region’s high altitude and cool nights allow the grapes to retain a ton of freshness, yielding vibrant, spicy red wines. Tastes like: Blackberry, nutmeg, smoke. How to drink: Lightly chilled with tacos al pastor or lean cuts of red meat.

A volcanic island chain 700 miles from mainland Spain, the Canary Islands are remote. This red wine illustrates that better than any other. It comes from a range of indigenous grapes, which grow untrained (wildly on the ground) on a steep slope on vines upwards of 200 years old. The result? A peppery, mineral-driven red that’s the most concentrated wine in Envínate's lineup.

Taganan is made from a whole host of red grape varieties native to the Canary Islands. Some of them remain unidentified, but all of them share a proximity to the Atlantic. Together, they yield a wine that's juicy, savory, and smoky – a perfect year-round red. Tastes like: Blackberries, black pepper, crackling fire. How to drink: Alongside roasted or grilled meats.

This bright red is a relatively new bottling from Envínate. On the Canary Islands, Roberto Santana hand-harvests very old vines of local grape varieties to craft a lithe, floral, slightly wild red wine. Enjoy it lightly chilled.

If you’re ever unsure what we mean when we call a white wine ‘salty’, ‘smoky’, or ‘savory’, this bottle is it. Envínate makes it from 100-year-old listan blanco vines a couple thousand feet above the Atlantic on the Canary Island of Tenerife.

Barbera doesn’t get better than this. Not only is it made by one of the world’s greatest red winemakers, but it comes from a vineyard that yields the most collectible wines in all of Italy. While barbera is generally regarded as a solid pizza wine, this is a more serious proposition. Extended aging, a legendary vineyard, and Roberto Conterno’s classic winemaking yield a bright red with structure and depth typically reserved for the region’s best nebbiolo.

An hour’s drive east of our favorite white winemakers in Italy, Marko Fon hunts down old and abandoned vineyards in Slovenia. Using only local grape varieties, he makes textured, salty white wines that are a bit cloudy and totally distinct. This malvasia, which he ferments on the skins for a short time to add depth and aromatics, is an ideal window into Marko’s house style. Tastes like: Apricot, sage, chamomile, sea salt. How to drink: Chilled with cheese and charcuterie, or pretty much anything from the ocean.

Few, if any, German winemakers crafted Kabinett - a delicate, ethereal, slightly off-dry style of riesling - as well as than the late Daniel Vollenweider. This is an seriously well-made wine from one of the Mosel's unsung stars.

Vollenweider is an insider’s estate in the Mosel region of Germany. Following in the footsteps of the late Daniel Vollenweider, Moritz Hoffman is making exceptional old-vine riesling. Tart, herbal, and smoky, 'Felsenfest' showcases Moritz’s preternatural feel for dry wines.

This remarkably complex dry riesling comes from the husband-and-wife team of Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler. In the Mosel region of Germany, they make fresh, focused white wines that punch well above their weight for the price. None more so than this deeply textured riesling from the lithe, pure 2022 vintage.

Konstantin Weiser and Alexandra Künstler make this bone-dry sparkling wine with old-vine riesling using the same method as Champagne. It's a lithe, refreshing, limited-release bubbly from one of the most exciting producers in the Mosel today.

The 'Cuvée N' – the N signifies no added sulfur – is bright and refreshing, while still spicy and powerful enough to stand up to red meat. Tastes like: Raspberry, roses, plum, black pepper. How to drink: Serve slightly chilled alongside burgers, heavier seafood dishes, or roast chicken.

The wine isn’t exposed to any oak, but the old vines and relatively warm growing site yield a dense, full-bodied White Burgundy. Tastes like: Ripe pear, brioche, jasmine. How to drink: Chilled with soft cheeses, spinach ravioli, or all types of shellfish.

Made from a blend of local grape varieties - primarily garnacha - less than 500 cases are produced each year. The juice only spends a few days with its skins, and is aged in steel, both of which lead to a fresh, juicy, aromatic red wine. Tastes like: Blueberry, roses, sea salt. The largest and southernmost cru in Beaujolais, Brouilly is an ideal bridge between the region’s easy-drinking reds and the deeply savory wines from villages a bit further north. This bottle from Sebastien Congretel illustrates that perfectly. After working under Beaujolais' rising-star Julien Sunier, Sebastien ventured out on his own and launched L'Epicurieux. He makes this organic bottling with no added sulfur, leading to a vibrant and refreshing red. Tastes like: Wild raspberry, smoke, vanilla. How to drink: Chilled with grilled chicken and sausages, or a picnic spread in the park.
Niederberg is a particularly cool growing site, yielding a ‘Premier Cru’ riesling that’s fine-tuned with bright citrus, herbal, and mineral notes.

Emrich-Schönleber is one of Germany’s very best producers of dry riesling. Their style, especially in 2022, is lithe and cutting yet powerfully concentrated. Niederberg is a particularly cool growing site, yielding a Kabinett that's rounded and powerfully aromatic, while still precise and mineral.

‘Halenberg’ is the top wine in the Emrich-Schönleber lineup, which makes it one of Germany's greatest bottles of dry riesling. Deep and dense, this is a wine with concentration and structure that draws comparisons to Keller.

His ‘A Liberdade’ is on the right side of natural, meaning a hand-crafted white that’s deep and lively yet crisp and focused.

There are a lot of impressive family trees in the world of wine. However, few compare to the Corsini family, which has nine centuries of history in Tuscany, including an ancestor who was pope, another who was a saint, and another who commissioned the Trevi Fountain in Rome. Over most of that timespan, they’ve been making wine at Villa Le Corti. Today, Duccio Corsini crafts this fresh, elegant take on Chianti from organic sangiovese a few miles outside of Florence. Tastes like: Red plum, violets, cracked black pepper. How to drink: Pair with eggplant parm, spaghetti pomodoro, or really anything

Name a marquee wine region, and Pedro Parra has likely consulted for its best producers. From Roulot and Liger Belair to Marco Marengo and Comando G. But his eponymous project isn't based in Burgundy or Barolo. It's located 500 km south of Santiago in Chile. There in his hometown of Concepción, Pedro is the force behind a winemaking movement you could call the ‘New Chile’. Pedro has a passion for terroir (he literally has his PhD in the field), and he focuses it on the isolated granite soils of southern Chile. Using native grape varieties, he produces fresh, exceptionally drinkable red wines.

Teobaldo Rivella and his wife, Maria, make just two wines from one vineyard in Barbaresco. That vineyard, however, happens to be Montestefano, home to some of the greatest dirt in all of Piedmont, and their red wines are as compelling as they are scarce. Rivella is an old-school producer, but while their nebbiolo has density and a deeply savory quality, it’s also fresh, silky, and refined. In other words, it’s absolutely delicious.

wine: Domaine de la Renière, Saumur Rouge 'Cabernet Franc Signature' 2018
notes: 2018 was Thibault Masse’s very first vintage at the helm of Domaine de la Renière. Taste the chenin and cabernet franc that he produced, and it’s clear that the future of this historic Loire property is very bright. Immediately converting to organics and avoiding any new oak, Thibault lets his high-elevation, limestone vineyards shine through in his wines. For this red, that means a lifted, savory wine with cab franc’s herbal, peppery notes clearly on display. Tastes like: Raspberry, violets, green bell pepper. How to drink: Ideal with steak fajitas, eggplant parm, or all kinds of BBQ.

wine: Domaine Didier Fornerol, Côte de Nuits-Villages 2018
notes: In Burgundy, the quality of a wine and the prestige of the vineyard it comes from tend to be closely linked. Those 13th century monks knew what they were doing. There are outliers, however, and chief among them are the wines of Didier Fornerol. Fornerol feels like insider’s Burgundy. None of his bottlings carry glitzy classifications, but all of them provide a pristine window into savory, old-school Burgundy. That very much goes for today’s red. It’s spicy and deeply textured, a collectible wine that you can and should enjoy as often as possible.

Sage, menthol, licorice, spice, tobacco, and incense are woven throughout a core dark red and blue fruit.

Onto the lighter side of things, here, Grignolino – the ultimate Piemontese 'chillable red' – gets the serious Rinaldi treatment while still maintaining the variety's innate levity. Crushed flowers, spice, and sweet, red-toned fruit are all nicely lifted, with added elemetns of singed orange rind, Angostura bitters and menthol. The palate is fine, fresh, light and taut with a cool finish that binds everything into perfect harmony. Served with a light chill, this will make for a serious warm weather red.

wine: Orsi San Vito Posca Bianca NV
notes: The Posca Bianca is a still take on Pignoletto (with a bit of Alionza, Albana and Malvasia), crafted in a style Federico dubs vino perpetuo . Drawn from a multi-vintage, solera-style tank that includes every vintage back to 2010, each bottling continues a never-ending blend. Combining the waxy and herbal characters of mature Pignoletto with the bright fruit and floral freshness of younger vintages, the Posca rolls out elderberry, white peach and gooseberry, kept in check by the grape’s trademark salty, nutty backbone. A trattoria-style wine of real intrigue — easy to drink, anything but simple

wine: Vino di Anna Sfuso di Anna Rosso 2022
notes: A bright, easy-going Etna red that wears its name with a wink— ‘sfuso’ may mean ‘bulk wine,’ or the kind you fill your own jug with down at the local cantina, but there’s nothing commonplace about it. Mostly old, bush-vine Nerello Mascalese with a scattering of Nerello Cappuccio, Grenache, and local whites, it’s fermented partly in clay qvevri and aged in chestnut barrels. Things are never boring chez Vino di Anna, as the final blend pulls from the estate’s 2022 field blend, enlivened with a splash of Palmento Rosso and just a dash Jeudi 15 Rosato for lift. Only the second bottling of this cuvee after the launch of this label in 2021, ‘Jeudi 15’ is a blend of organically grown Carricante, Catarratto, and Grecanico from high-elevation northern vineyards. It’s bright and saline, with ripe lemon and pineapple cutting through a taut, mineral frame. Dry, with a fleshy mid-palate full of yellow peach, citrus zest, and wildflowers, it finishes with a tropical lift and electric acidity.

A striking Etna red drawn from two vineyards on opposite sides of the winery, one ancient, one young, both alive with volcanic intensity. Half comes from Vigna Jules, a 90-year-old bush-vine parcel farmed biodynamically, its deep silty soils yielding dark cherry, plum, and spice with brooding depth and fine, firm tannins. The other half, from Vigna Gaspard, an amphitheater of terraces planted in 2014 from massale selections, brings lift and crunch —wild strawberry, blueberry, and orange blossom flashing through volcanic earth. Charged with volcanic verve, this vintage comes from a cooler year, giving it tighter lines and sharper edges. A blend of organically farmed, native Sicilian varieties gathered from four distinct corners of the island (Grillo from Marsala, Cataratto from Alcamo, etc.), each parcel is fermented on its own before being united at Anna and Eric’s cellar high on Etna’s northern slopes. The nose opens with white flowers and citrus oil; the palate with lemon zest, grapefruit pith, and sea-spray salinity. This is a wine that is at once dangerously drinkable and wildly iconoclastic, yet leveled with vi

The Palmento Rosso – a nod to their 300-year-old traditional Etnean wine building – is true to style: while light and fresh, it has the pronounced fruit intensity of a great Etna red, full of cherries, brambly wild raspberry, macerated strawberries, blood orange. There are floral notes, along with a distinctive minerality indicative of the volcanic terroir. Acidity is well-defined and balanced, the finish is persistent and refreshing. Nerello Mascalese makes up 90% of this blend, along with small percentages of Nerello Cappuccio, Grecanico, Carricante, and Minnella Bianca; as old-school as it

Bianco 'G' is Vino di Anna's flagship white wine, the 'G' here standing for Grecanico (known as Garganega up north in the Veneto) from 60+-year-old vines, and a small portion of Carricante (grape varieties that proved resistant to downy mildew, which decimated Etna’s vineyards of Nerello Mascalese in 2023.) The Grecancio is macerated on the skins for four days and matured in stainless steel; the rest is whole bunch, direct pressed and aged in chestnut barrels before blending all together. notes: It's time to get to know Vitovska, an indigenous grape of Friuli and Slovenia (which were, of course, one and the same), whose profile is inextricably linked to its environment. Grown in the Carso district of Italy near Trieste, between mountains (the Alps) and sea (the Adriatic), it’s a variety that marries the identities of these climatic forces effortlessly. Meaning 'cluster,' Togliana's 'L’Arsin' is a classically-styled Carema, made from 100% Nebbiolo from the various small estate owned parcels. The fermentation is carried out with native yeasts in stainless steel tanks. Aging takes place in large French oak casks (1,000L) for 15 months, plus in stainless steel for 2 months before release. A classic alpine Nebbiolo, juicy, vibrant and loaded with small berry aromas, followed by wild herbs and forest floor. Fine tannins and the typical mineral backbone of Carema close on the finish. 2000 bottles made. Carema, nestled at the foothills of the Alps n

An unassuming but spot-on introduction to Valtellina Nebbiolo, and to the new wave of the Balgera winery. 20% is 2019 unoaked Nebbiolo, 80% is 2016 Nebbiolo aged in large cask, all subject to shorter macerations. A juicy, and bright mountain red (not unsuited for a light chill!), loaded with wild strawberries, faded red flowers, thyme and freshly ripe blackberries. Silky and smooth tannins give this great structure and keep it super easy-going.

Legendary Mauro Franchino and his nephew Alberto Raviciotti farm a scant three hectares practicing sustainable viticulture. They select only their best Nebbiolo to make their wines in their tiny winery in the center of Gattinara. On a typical year, they use only 50% of their crop, while the remaining 50% is sold to other producers. Nestled in the pre-Alpi hills north of Novara and Vercelli, Gattinara has for centuries been known for austere, age-worthy Nebbiolo, locally known as Spanna, Gattinara’s reputation pre-dates even Barolo and Barbaresco, but the cultivation of vines here was progressi

Made from 100% Marzemino grown in Trentino’s La Rua vineyard, this is a faithful expression of one of northern Italy’s most characterful native grapes —delicate, fragrant, and effortlessly drinkable. Violets, red cherries, and wild raspberries rise from the glass with vivid clarity, accented by a faint note of spice and crushed stone. The palate is bright and supple, carrying flavors of fresh plum, sour cherry, and red currant, balanced by lively acidity and just a whisper of fine-grained tannins. wine: Torre dei Beati Giocheremo con i Fiori Pecorino d'Abruzzo 2023
notes: “We are playing with flowers” is the perfect title for a wine that smells of elderflowers and beeswax, and has a remarkable amount of both texture and tart typical Pecorino acidity on the palate.

notes: Fresh and classic, this wine opens with delicate notes of green apple, citrus blossom, and a hint of freshly baked bread. Light and effortless, the flavors are crisp and clean, carried by fine bubbles and bright acidity. An easy, enjoyable sip that showcases its understated charm with refreshing precision.

wine: Divella Gussago Rose de Saignee Dosaggio Zero 2019

Uninhibited by any addition of dosage and hemmed together with a soft touch of tannin and marked salinity, on the palate it is sleek and fine, with pronounced freshness and a creamy bubble. Reeling with wild strawberries, red flowers, custard and dry pastry, this is a sparkling wine of substance and elegance.

wine: Divella Gussago Blanc de Blancs Dosaggio Zero 2021 Magnum 1.5L

With only 1g/L of residual sugar present in the bottle, and a whopping 33 months on the lees, the wine is racy and full on the palate, with big bursts of green apple, lemon zest, pear, and brioche. 100% Barbera (estate fruit from Cellario’s own biodynamic vineyards). 10 days skin maceration gives it good extraction but still keeps it juicy and fresh. Aging is in cement. “Quantobasta” means “just enough”, meaning you can have as little or as much as you want - the perfect amount!

aromas: Cranberry, Star Anise, Smoke, Flint, Thyme, Graphite
notes: Nestled between Etna's Passopisciaro and Solicchiata, sourced from 80 year old vines, emerges an elegant 100% Nerello Mascalese by Rocca Coeli. Aromatics of smoke, flint, dark currant, rose and Mediterranean scrub gives way to layers of morello cherry, cranberry, star anise, thyme and graphite on the palate. Packed with elegance and mineral tension along with fine tannins and crisp acidity this Etna Rosso pairs well with oily fish like sardines, tuna, and swordfish, as well as heavier, meaty dishes.

wine: Podere Il Saliceto Bi Fri Frizzante 2024
notes: 80% Trebbiano di Modena, 20% Sauvignon, ‘Bi Fri' stands for Bianco Frizzante , but also 'Be Free' - and who are we to argue with this light, lively, and lip-smacking offering? Direct press juice with natural primary fermentation in stainless steel, and secondary fermentation in bottle with must from original harvest. Minimal added sulfur and no filtering or fining. White flowers, grapefruit and citrus pith, and tomato leaf dominate an über-fresh and vivacious mouthful of rustic Emilia fizz. A killer wine perfect for any sunny occasion.

wine: Erpacrife Nebbiolo Metodo Classico Dossage Zero 2019

“Mofete” which means “it’s erupting” in Sicilian dialect is an Etna Rosso comprised of 80% Nerello Mascalese and 20% Nerello Cappuccio from various estate vineyards in Passopisciaro. Each plot is fermented separately with native yeasts in stainless steel. A selection of the resulting batches is then assembled and aged 50% in stainless steel, 50% in 50HL Slavonian neutral oak. Juicy, wild berry aromas are wrapped in the signature mineral notes typical of volcanic soils. Grilled, smoked herbs close a delicious finish.

wine: Roeno Collezione di Famiglia Riesling Renano 2018
notes: There are less than 450 acres of Rhine Riesling planted in Italy, and the majority are located in Trentino and Alto Adige thanks to the strong influence of German and Austrian winemaking. Roeno’s Riesling vineyards are located on the slopes of Mount Baldo, which stands between Garda Lake and the Adige Valley. “Collezione di Famiglia” is made only in the best vintages from a strict selection of the best grapes. Bright acidity, great minerality, superb freshness, light tannins — what else could you want in a late summer wine? Weingut Pranzegg is a small 3.5 hectare family estate nestled in the surrounding mountain foothills of the town of Bozen in Südtirol (AKA Alto Adige), just 50 km south of the Austrian border. The winery has been in the hands of the Gojer family for three generations. Martin took over the estate in 2008 and started the conversion to biodynamic farming straight away; he also stopped selling to the local cooperatives, a bold move in an area where 90% of all grapes are bottled by coo

Not your mom's Pinot Grigio! An brilliant and unexpected take on the varietal. High elevation grapes are picked over the course of several passes in the vineyard for optimal quality and ripeness. Whole bunch maceration over a couple of weeks results in a deep amber/dark rose color, stunning aromatics and a pluck on the palate that leaves us smiling each and every time.

Pinot Blanc needs certain things to truly thrive: complex soils, perfect sun exposure and a good breeze. Dornach, sitting at an elevation of 350 meters, in the idyllic Alto Adige region, is perfectly positioned to grow world class Pinot Blanc, and the farm’s embrace of the natural world and deft touch in the cellar creates a wine with intense, crystalline personality and passion. This cuvee blends Chardonnay (40%) for lovely added texture and complexity.

A stunner, Dornach's vins de soif (thirst wine) is an alpine Pinot Noir that bursts with pleasure and personality. It’s elegant and lovely but don’t let the almost translucent hue fool you -- this is serious wine from a top estate full of pure fresh fruit. Fresh picked strawberries, rhubarb and love.

A new cuvée from mountain maestro and dedicated biodynamic vigeron Martin Gojer just arrived; 'Elysion' is 100% Pinot Bianco (aka Weissburgunder in these German-speaking parts) and marries the natural weight and siftness of the variety with zippy notes of lemongrass and wild herbs. Fleshy stone fruit and a mineral spine add depth.

Four generations of the Pichler family live in the same small stone farmhouse home, farm the same vines their family has been tending to almost a millennium, and produce organically farmed, classic examples of Südtirol Schiava, Lagrein, and a small amount of French varieties. Located in Eppan, in the heart of the Südtirol – Italy's only Deutsche speaking region – the architecture, cuisine, and culture in this area is Austrian, and the region's reds have less in common with the powerful, sanguine, tannic reds of Tuscany or Piedmont that define Italy in the minds of many wine lovers, than the th

100% biodynamically-farmed Müller-Thurgau from super high elevation – 720 meters! Elegant and easy drinking, with a golden yellow hue and refreshing palate of bright, spicy fruit, and tight minerality. Incredibly aromatic, as a delightful blend of apple and wildflower create an intriguing and unforgettable Alpine experience. Textured with layers of flavors that show orchard fruit in all its glory while notes of yeast and vibrant acidity keep the wine fresh.

Another wonder from ‘Fizz Wizzard’ Matteo Furlani - dry, juicy and absolutely delicious. A field blend of native Dolomiti grapes Marzemino, Turca, and Negrara, full of spice, earth and red forest fruits throughout. Wild strawberry, crushed white peppercorn, and a distinctively herbaceous, bell peppery streak are buoyed by tiny, tight fizz and mineral drive. Fresh and bright as a summer’s morning in the mountains of Trentino! As always, very serious for the appellation, with pure cherry, bark and walnut character as well as a hint of dark chocolate. Medium-bodied, firm and focused, with integrated tannins and a long and flavorful finish. The fruit is generous and primary, and the wine ends with mildly chalky tannins.

wine: Domini Del Leone Prosecco Brut NV
notes: A Prosecco from Veneto's oldest organic producer. Unlike the filtered, tank-fermented proseccos that are common today, it follows the older col fondo tradition, a nod to the way frizzante wines were made in many areas of Italy before modern methods took over. F ruit-forward notes of green apple and fresh-cut pear meet salty undertones from the distinctive Caranto soil.

wine: Fratelli Alessandria Barolo San Lorenzo di Verduno 2021
aromas: Blood Orange, Orange Peel, Rose Petal, White Pepper, Chalk, Slate, Saline, Mint
notes: Vittore Alessandria's 2021 Barolos are hugely promising. The Sarn Lorenzo is a wine of translucence, elegance, and finesse. Bright acids cut through a core of red and purple fruit, chalk, slate, crushed stone, and white pepper. Rose petal, blood orange peel, and mint resonate on the high-toned, intensely saline finish.

wine: Fasoli Gino La Corte Del Pozzo Bardolino 2024

His wines are complex and classically styled, but always offer plenty of truffle/floral intrigue to compliment the instantly gratifying dark fruit. There is no modern technology in the cellar. The most impactful "technique" is that Gianluigi refuses to release wines until they're truly ready to drink. Malvasia, Ortrugo, and Marsanne dominate the blend with the addition of 25% 'unknown varietals;' the Dinavolo offers a dense and brawny profile highlighted by apricot skin, marmalade, white balsamic, candied citrus pith, and bay leaf all woven through unashamedly full and luscious mouthfeel drawn from a number of month spent on skins. A wine that demands time, air, temperature and a big beautiful hunk of porchetta.

Don Fausto Spumante is a sparkling wine made from Malvasia and Chardonnay. Very aromatic nose with typical floral and fruity hints of Malvasia to which are added hazelnuts, sage, butter, and mineral from aging on the lees. Fresh and creamy mouthfeel with savory finish and nice structure.

wine: Il Roccolo di Monticelli Monticelli Rosso 2022
notes: A blend of Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella, Molinara, and Oseleta from limestone soil, this is Valpolicella at its more lithe and playful end. Grapes see a whopping 90-day maceration but you'd never guess it here - no signs of over-extraction, just bright, justly restrained red fruit. It then ages 8 months further in steel. A lighter-styled red, with echoes of the Loire Valley, Silvia's rosso is delicate in body with aromas of white pepper and geranium alongside notes of cherry and raspberry. wine: Il Roccolo di Monticelli Obelix Bianco 2023
notes: Only the grapes of the oldest vines of Garganega are used for this cuvee and are carefully harvested from select bunches. After spontaneous fermentation, with some whole cluster maceration, the wine is aged for several months in terracotta amphora. This is pure, old-world wine making; no clarification, filtration or addition of sulfur. What results is a bright, light orange wine bursting with citrus notes and a touch of flinty herbaceousness. You might even consider pairing it with Obelix’s favorite dish: wild boar!

Marco’s ‘Tufaliccio’ Rosso is one of those seemingly humble wines that possesses that rare ‘transportational’ quality. wine: Berucci Mola da Piedi Cesanese del Piglio 2019
notes: Aged in one single 300L clay amphorae, this is as as pristine, unadorned and manicured expression of Cesanese as you will find. Fruit is sourced from one small vineyard of very old vines, accessible only by foot; once picked it is foot-trodden and fermented in open-tops wooden vats. Delicate, dried purple flowers, perfectly ripe plummy fruit and a sense of… life that seems to evade comprehension. While this is the pinnacle of Maria's production, in her own words, this is not a wine intended to age. A new addition – for us! – to the Mattioli's seemingly inexhaustible lineup, 'Buscaia' is a tale of two Malvasias: a direct-press white wine obtained from two different strains of the variety, the traditional strain with a tight bunch and thick skin, and the “Candia” strain with a loose bunch, and a large and delicate grape. Both are harvested at the beginning of October and are vinified through spontaneous fermentation in stainless steel tanks; no sulfur is added at any point. aromas: Blackberry, Raspberry, Black Cherry, Sour Cherry, Violet, Black Pepper, Cinnamon
notes: 100% Ciliegiolo from 15-50 years old vines; spontaneous fermentation with wild yeasts on the skins for 6 days in cement vats, then aged in steel all winter, and bottled during the waning moon in early March. Red-violet in color, with aromas of black cherry, sour cherry, black pepper, a shake of cinnamon, a trace of wild violets and warm terracotta. Blackberry, raspberry, red currant, and balsamic notes are met with bright acidity and good tannins. Plush, pure, and bright, and very suited for a light chill.

Even in a sometimes "challenging" vintage in Tuscany, Veronica's Chianti DOCG s a wave of dark and red cherry fruit, pleasantly chewy, and endlessly refreshing on the palate, with haunting blue flowers and tobacco on the nose and a flavor architecture perfectly framed by dusty tannins. Veronica recently revived the property's century-old underground concrete fermenters, which helps author this wine's irresistible freshness and vivid fruit. The end result is everything we want from a Chianti vino da tavola.

Fongoli's 2016 Fracanton Montefalco Sagrantino is a wine of remarkable precision and depth. It exhibits the varietal's hallmark intensity—robust tannins, concentrated layers of dark cherry and plum, and mineral undertones that reflect the limestone-rich soils of Umbria. This vintage demonstrates excellent structure and aging capacity, making it particularly suited for cellaring or pairing with substantial dishes such as braised meats and aged charcuterie.

Born on the volcanic slopes of Mount Somma—the ancient inner cone of Vesuvius—this captivating white from Cantine Olivella channels the raw energy of Campania’s landscape. Crafted entirely from Catalanesca, a grape once relegated to table fruit, Katà has shed its humble origins to emerge as a wine of precision and place. Fragrant notes of lemon zest, crisp pear, and wild herbs rise from the glass, underpinned by a briny whisper of sea spray and a streak of volcanic minerality. wine: Durin Riviera Ligure di Ponente Vermentino 2023

Aromas of ripe citrus and honey, mint, and a touch of sea salt dominate this medium-bodied, textured, refined Campanian white. Since the end of the nineteenth century, the Troisi family has championed the wines of Irpina, a historic vine-growing area in northern Campania. Vadiaperti’s high-altitude vineyards and pure volcanic soils combine for southern Italian white wines of impeccable finesse, freshness and character.

Made from the little-known Grignolino grape, this light red wine is made for drinking not meditation. That is, however, not to say that great care was not taken in the making of this little gem: hand harvested organic grapes are spontaneously fermented, sulfur additions are kept to an absolute minimum and neither fining nor filtration are employed. Cranberry-hued, translucent, and just a shade or two darker than rosé (the skin of Grignolino contains little pigment), E Grino! is the paragon of a light-drinking red and surprisingly versatile for even chillier climes. Now the winery is run by two sisters, Roberta and Alice, whose great-great-great-grandfather Niccolo was the first certified winemaker in the Abruzzo region, gaining a diploma from the Royal School of Conegliano Veneto in 1889. wine: Giuseppe Cipolla Passofonduto Le Robbe Rosso 2022
notes: Warmly integrated with soft black tea-like tannins, black licorice, citrus zest and an almost pottery-like, earthen tone that just feels Sicilian, the Passofonduto is balanced with bright, earthy plum, and a host of savory, mineral aromas and flavors. This wine may emerge in the coming years as one of Sicily's truly great, standard-bearing wines!

'In Chino' is made according to an old recipe from the Langhe region of Piemonte featuring Cinchona root (Cinchona Officinalis), Cinchona calisaya bark, quassia, and a special blend of herbs and spices. Intense, bitter and honey notes with hints of toasted clove, eucalyptus, cinnamon and coriander open on the nose. These flavors evolve on the palate into a yin-and-yang of bitter and sweet that coats the tongue; rhubarb, date, sultana, cloves, five spice and orange bitters are all present and there is a lovely, warm mouth-feel. An incredibly long, intense finish that is both dry and sweet.

We have stocked Drusian Prosecco since day one. A customer favorite, due to its versatility, price and flavor profile, this is a dry, delicately fruity and crisp Prosecco that is perfect for any occasion, whether mixing for cocktails or simply as an aperitif. Creamy and rich, this delivers a distant softness. The mouthfeel is enhanced by flavors of peach, citrus and honey.

Talk about fresh as a daisy and firing on all cylinders! Derived entirely from the local specialty in Nerello Mascalese, the fruit sees a feather-light pressing before being transferred to concrete tanks for fermentation and aging. Equal parts vibrant, delicate and punchy; über-pretty cherry, raspberry, rose petal, cassis and sweet herbs bursting on the nose and palate, with a distinct core of savory, flinty minerality that harks to the wine’s volcanic home.

A beautiful shade of gold in the glass , this is all aromatic herbs, sea spray, and citrus fruits — it begs for sunshine, and a nice piece of fish.

Full of red roses, wild strawberries, raspberries, and Mediterrean herbs. Winemaker Antonio Basso represents the third generation of farmers from Ortovero, and tends some 259 separate, small vineyards on steep hillsides just three miles away from the azure Mediterranean as the crow flies. Here in the west of Sicily, where the soil is barren and full of limestone, the Sicilian white wine varieties Cataratto, Inzolia, and Zibibbo (Moscato d’Alexandria) grow extremely well. The Scala’s Cirò Rosso is fashioned entirely from Calabria’s most celebrated red varietal, Gaglioppo, a relatively thick-skinned grape known for producing rustic and savory wines. Imbued with an expected amount of ‘southern solar power,’ the wine’s boisterous nature and riper fruit characters are kept in check via a vinification that sees it raised entirely in a mixture of stainless steel and cement tanks. Concentrated and wild in its aromatics, there is an almost smoky amaro-meets-camphor-inflected red and black fruit quality that dominates the nose, with a distinctive purple flower overtone

wine: Marco de Bartoli Terzavia Metodo Classico 2020
notes: 'Terzavia,' or 'the third way,' showcases Marco’s ever evolving experimental and innovative spirit. This traditional method sparkler of 100% Grillo is pulled from 30 year old Guyot-trained vines. Fermentation begins in stainless steel tanks and continues for just 20% of the grapes in French oak barrels. Tirage (the drawing of the wine into bottles for a second fermentation) follows with fresh must instead of sugar, after which it goes to bottle for at least 18 months, always on its own lees and with zero dosage.
